title: Hong Kong Express EPOS
summary: Ordering website, iPhone app, till, kitchen display, delivery dispatch and AI phone line for a Chinese takeaway, all run from one backend.

brief: Hong Kong Express is a Chinese takeaway in Broomfield, Chelmsford. It needed one system to take orders from a website, a phone app and the counter, get them to the kitchen and out to drivers, and give the manager a view of the whole shop.

I built it in four parts: a customer ordering website, an iPhone app with a separate mode for staff and drivers, the in-shop software (till, kitchen display, dispatch map and manager dashboard), and a single backend that serves all of them.

built.title: Counter till
built.body: Staff take counter and phone orders on the till, charge cards through a Stripe Terminal reader and print receipts on the shop’s Epson printers. Dish names print in English and Chinese: I render the Chinese text as raster images because the printers can’t print Unicode. The till installs on a Windows 11 touchscreen from a branded installer and keeps itself up to date with signed updates.

built.title: Kitchen display
built.body: New orders appear as tickets on the kitchen screen, split into Live, Ready, Later and Done, and can be filtered by waiting or cooking and by collection or delivery. Cooks can sort oldest first or push late and priority tickets to the top, and the screen chimes when a new order arrives.

built.title: Delivery dispatch
built.body: Drivers use the staff mode in the mobile app to see their jobs, get directions and clock in and out, sharing their location while on shift. The manager sees every driver on a live map and assigns orders to them from there.

built.title: Ordering website and iPhone app
built.body: Customers browse the live menu with allergen filters, pay with Stripe or Apple Pay, collect loyalty rewards and track their order. Owners set collection and delivery wait times once, and the website and app quote the same estimate. On iPhone, order progress also shows as a Live Activity on the lock screen.

built.title: AI phone assistant
built.body: Calls go from Twilio to OpenAI’s live voice model. The assistant answers questions about the menu, prices, opening hours and delivery areas from live backend data, and can build a collection or delivery order and text the caller a one-time Stripe checkout link, so no card details are taken over the phone. Callers can check on an order after confirming a code sent to their mobile, and requests to change or refund an order go to staff as cases. The till shows who is ringing by matching the number against past orders.

architecture: One Rust backend (Axum and SQLx) serves the website, the mobile app and the in-shop software, and supervises background workers for orders, payments, notifications, delivery and loyalty.
Laravel handles migrations, seeding and part of the test suite. MySQL is the hosted database; the in-shop software can run against a local SQLite database.
The staff desktop app is a Tauri shell that starts the backend as a sidecar and only allows staff routes. New staff get a one-use, 24-hour setup link by email.
The phone line is a small Node service between Twilio and OpenAI that calls the backend for menu data, baskets and checkout links.
CI runs Rust formatting, Clippy and tests, PHP tests on SQLite and MySQL, dependency audits, a secret scan, the mobile checks, and builds and install-tests the Windows installer on every push.
outcome: Built and tested end to end, from the website to the kitchen printer.
The system became the starting point for Relay Clarity, which turns it into a product any takeaway can run.

title: Relay Clarity
summary: Restaurant software that gives each takeaway its own ordering website, apps, till, kitchen screens and AI phone line, all run from one platform.

brief: Independent takeaways usually stitch together a till from one company, a website from another and a delivery app that takes a cut of every order. Relay Clarity gives each business one system instead: its own branded ordering website and app, a till, kitchen screens, a manager dashboard, delivery dispatch and an AI receptionist that answers the phone.

It grew out of the system I built for Hong Kong Express. I turned that single-restaurant build into a platform where every business is set up from a pack of its own menu, branding and settings, with no business-specific code in the product.

built.title: One system per restaurant
built.body: Each business gets a hosted ordering website, an iPhone app built from the same Expo codebase, and the RelayClarity Business desktop app for the till, kitchen screen, manager dashboard and receipt printing. Customers pay into the restaurant’s own Stripe account through Stripe Connect, so the money never passes through the platform.

built.title: A till that keeps working offline
built.body: If the internet drops, the till keeps taking cash orders. They are written to an append-only log encrypted with AES-256-GCM and replayed with their original idempotency keys when the connection returns, so each order lands exactly once.

built.title: Updates that never interrupt service
built.body: Installed tills update themselves from signed packages, with a beta channel, staged rollouts, a minimum version and a kill switch. Each device keeps a fixed rollout bucket, so widening a rollout never drops devices that already have it. The app won’t restart while a receipt is printing, and if a new version fails to start twice it rolls itself back and reports it.

built.title: AI receptionist
built.body: Calls go from Twilio to OpenAI’s live voice model over SIP. The receptionist answers questions about the menu, opening hours and delivery, and the till shows who is ringing alongside their past orders. Every call is checked against a kill switch, daily cost caps per business and for the whole platform, and a limit on simultaneous calls; refused calls go to the restaurant or voicemail. Taking orders by phone is off by default.

built.title: Kitchen and delivery
built.body: Orders arrive on the kitchen screen as timed tickets. The manager assigns delivery orders to drivers on a live map, drivers get their jobs and directions in the staff app, and customers follow their order from the kitchen to their door.

architecture: A Rust backend (Axum and SQLx, on MySQL or SQLite) serves every business from one deployment, with tenant hosts, an encrypted secret store, usage metering, custom domains, backups and scheduled deletion.
Each business is described by a pack: menu, branding, opening hours, delivery zones and which features are on. Build checks fail if one business’s name or branding leaks into shared code.
Refactoring the original takeaway build into this template was checked screen by screen: 416 of 416 screenshots stayed pixel-identical across desktop, phone, light and dark.
The desktop app is Tauri and only works once paired to a business with a one-time setup code; each staff role sees only its own pages.
The phone line runs as a separate Node service between Twilio and OpenAI, and a prepaid gateway in Rust admits and bills each call.
outcome: The product site is live at relayclarity.com, and restaurants can apply for a quote.
The hosted platform is in pre-launch testing.

title: Bear Lane
summary: Online shop for custom printed clothing, with a design tool where customers place their own text, clipart and images on a garment.

brief: Bear Lane sells printed clothing. The owner wanted customers to design their own garments online and pay, with each order landing in an admin panel that has everything needed to print and ship it. Products, prices and the homepage also had to be editable without touching code.
I built the shop, the design tool, checkout and shipping, customer accounts and the admin panel.

built.title: Design tool
built.body: Customers pick a garment and colour, then add text, clipart and their own uploaded images to the front, back or either sleeve. Each element can be moved, resized and cropped inside a marked print area, and designs can be saved to the customer’s account to finish later.

built.title: Checkout and shipping
built.body: Checkout takes card and wallet payments through Stripe, as well as PayPal, and applies discount codes. Shipping rates come from Shippo, using a parcel size estimated from what’s in the basket. Before payment, checkout re-checks the delivery price and availability, and the accepted quote is stored with the order, so the admin can buy the postage label without leaving the panel.

built.title: Admin panel
built.body: The owner manages products, nested categories, prices, carriers and parcel sizes, discount codes, tax settings and the size guide. The homepage is edited in place: any text, image or section can be changed, moved, added or removed, with undo, and goes live on save. The same panel handles orders and returns, and shows sales, refunds, best-selling products and reviews for a chosen date range.

built.title: Accounts, chat and moderation
built.body: Customers sign in with email or with Google, Apple or Facebook, and keep addresses, saved designs, a wishlist and order history. Live chat with the shop runs over Pusher, and chat messages and any text added to a design are checked with OpenAI’s moderation API before they’re accepted.

built.title: Every request reaches the owner
built.body: Support messages, quote requests, chat, returns, restock alerts and newsletter sign-ups all reach the owner’s inbox through a mail queue on Resend that retries failed sends.

architecture: Laravel 12 serves a React and TypeScript front end through Inertia.js.
The design tool is a React canvas; the finished design is exported as an image with html2canvas and stored with the order.
Stripe and PayPal take payments, Shippo provides rates and labels, and Pusher with Laravel Echo carries live chat.
Deployed on Railway from a Dockerfile. Shell scripts back up and restore the live database and uploaded files, and a pre-push check guards against losing them.

title: Vibyra
summary: Workspace for running AI coding agents like Claude Code and Codex side by side on your own computer, then picking the work up from an iPhone or handing it to the cloud.

brief: Coding agents like Claude Code and Codex run in a terminal on your own machine, which ties you to your desk. Vibyra puts several of them in one desktop workspace, lets you check on or continue that work from a phone, and can hand a project to a cloud computer so it keeps going while your laptop is shut.

It has four parts: the desktop app for Mac, Windows and Linux; a Rust host that pairs a phone with a computer; an iPhone app; and Vibyra Cloud, with accounts, billing and model access run from a Laravel backend.

built.title: Many agents, no lag
built.body: The desktop app runs Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI or any other command-line agent side by side in a grid of real terminals. Each terminal has its own reader thread in Rust and one shared flusher batches output for all of them: keystrokes echo straight away, heavy output is grouped into 16 ms batches, and hidden terminals buffer into a scrollback that replays when you come back.

built.title: Phone pairing, end-to-end encrypted
built.body: A phone pairs with a computer through a one-time invitation, and nothing is trusted until you approve the device’s key on the computer. Every frame is encrypted with the Noise protocol, compiled to WebAssembly for the phone, so the relay in between forwards traffic it can’t read. Only one device can type into a terminal at a time.

built.title: Handing work to the cloud
built.body: To move a project to Vibyra Cloud, the desktop app snapshots it into a shadow git repository, builds an incremental bundle and encrypts it so only that account’s cloud computer can open it. Changes coming back go through a three-way review before they touch your files. The server wakes the cloud machine when work arrives and stops it after five idle minutes, so you only pay for time in use.

built.title: Models, routing and billing
built.body: Pro plans include credit for every major model through OpenRouter, sold at cost. An Auto option sorts each prompt (front end, large codebase, review and so on) and picks a suitable model allowed by the plan. Billing runs on Stripe with integer units and signed compute leases, and free usage has a platform-wide daily cap.

built.title: Agents and benchmarks
built.body: Agent ‘teammates’ keep a brief, notes and skills, and scheduled routines run on their own. A remote MCP gateway lets agents use outside tools while blocking requests to private networks. The public benchmarks page combines 23 independent leaderboards into one score per model, compared at matching reasoning effort.

architecture: Desktop: Tauri 2 with a React 19 and xterm.js interface. Terminal sessions, agent detection, previews and cloud sync live in Rust crates with no webview dependency.
Host: a Rust workspace (transport, server and engine) that runs terminals and agent sessions on the computer; a small Node relay matches phones to computers.
Backend: Laravel on Railway with PostgreSQL, serving the website, accounts, billing, downloads, the model gateway and the benchmarks page.
Cloud: one Fly.io machine per account in London, with an encrypted volume and S3-compatible storage for project bundles.
iPhone: Expo and React Native, keeping device keys in SecureStore.
outcome: Vibyra Desktop is available from vibyra.net for Mac, Windows and Linux, with signed in-app updates.
Free and Pro plans are live, with Pro billed through Stripe.
The iPhone app is in testing and not yet on the App Store.

title: AI Voice Assistant
summary: Raspberry Pi desk assistant written in Rust: say the wake word, ask something, and it answers out loud, checks the weather or sets timers.

brief: A voice assistant that sits on a desk: a Raspberry Pi with a touchscreen, a microphone and speakers. I wanted something that wakes on its own name, starts answering quickly, does a few useful things, and says plainly when a request is beyond it.
I built the first version in Python, then rewrote it in Rust in August 2026.

built.title: Offline wake word
built.body: Wake-word detection runs on the Pi with rustpotter, so no audio leaves the device until you say the phrase. A train-wake command records six samples of your own voice to build the model, and tapping the on-screen orb also wakes it.

built.title: Listening
built.body: After a chime it records with an adaptive energy gate that stops after a stretch of silence. It keeps listening for a few seconds after each answer so you can carry on talking, and tapping the screen while it speaks cuts it off.

built.title: Streaming replies
built.body: Speech is transcribed with gpt-4o-mini-transcribe and answered by gpt-4o-mini. I split the reply into sentences as it streams in and send each one to text-to-speech straight away, so it starts talking before the full answer has arrived.

built.title: Tools
built.body: The model can call tools for weather (Open-Meteo), timers that chime and count down on screen, volume control and the local time and date. For things it can’t do, such as music or smart-home control, it says so.

built.title: Touchscreen interface
built.body: A fullscreen egui app shows an animated orb that reacts to your voice, a clock, running timers and a live transcript. A systemd user service starts it when the Pi boots.

architecture: Microphone audio comes in through cpal and feeds the wake-word detector; after a wake, a voice-activity gate cuts out the spoken request.
The request goes to OpenAI speech-to-text, then to a chat model that can call local tools, with a trimmed conversation history kept between turns.
A sentence splitter feeds streaming text-to-speech, and rodio plays the audio.
Tokio runs the network calls, and the egui interface reads shared state over channels.

title: Vehicle Service Booking API
summary: Booking API for a vehicle service centre that enforces opening hours, VIN checks and no double bookings, built as a take-home exercise.

brief: This was a take-home technical exercise. I was given a .NET solution with empty API, application, data and test projects and a written brief, and built the booking system across those layers.

The API lists service types and lets a customer book, move or cancel an appointment. It enforces the brief’s rules: weekdays only, on the hour, between 08:00 and 17:00, a 17-character VIN, and no two bookings for the same service in the same slot.

built.title: Booking rules
built.body: I put every rule in one validation method in the application service, shared by create and update, so the endpoints only turn results into HTTP responses. Updates skip the availability check when the slot hasn’t changed, so an appointment can’t clash with itself.

built.title: Double-booking guard
built.body: A unique database index on service type and start time backs up the service-level check. If two requests race for the same slot, I catch the constraint failure and return the same ‘slot already booked’ message rather than a server error.

built.title: Data layer
built.body: I wrote EF Core models with length limits, a check that durations are positive and a restricted foreign key, plus repositories with paging and no-tracking reads. A migration creates the schema, and seeding adds three service types only if the table is empty.

built.title: Tests
built.body: Nine NUnit tests with Moq repository fakes cover the required cases (VIN length, business hours, weekends, taken slots, a valid booking and cancellation) and two I added: on-the-hour starts and unchanged updates.

architecture: Four projects: API (minimal API endpoints and Swagger UI), Application (DTOs, services and validation), Data (EF Core, repositories, migrations and seeding) and Tests.
Endpoints return 201, 200, 204, 400 with a plain error message, or 404. Only DTOs leave the API; database entities stay inside.
On startup the app applies migrations to a local SQLite database and seeds it.

title: Service Priority AI
summary: Machine-learning triage for council service requests: rates each one low, medium or high, explains why, and leaves the call to a person.

brief: Councils get more service requests than they can look at at once, and some, such as a fire risk in a home with children, need attention first. This project predicts a priority for each request and shows the reasons to an officer, who makes the final call.

It’s a portfolio project on synthetic data. I built the whole path around the model: data generation, training, an API, a dashboard, Azure deployment files, and the governance documents a public body would ask for.

built.title: Model
built.body: A scikit-learn pipeline combines one-hot encoded case fields, scaled numbers such as days open and previous contacts, and TF-IDF features from the free-text description, feeding a class-balanced logistic regression. I trained it on 25,000 synthetic cases.

built.title: Prediction API
built.body: A FastAPI service with typed schemas: /predict returns the priority, confidence scores and the factors behind it, and /chat is a grounded assistant that explains scoring and fairness without calling an external LLM. Health, metrics and batch-scoring endpoints are covered by pytest.

built.title: Triage dashboard
built.body: A React app with a public service portal and an operator console showing live triage, model metrics, fairness checks, SHAP explanations, batch scoring and governance, with the assistant docked at the side.

built.title: Azure MLOps and governance
built.body: Azure ML CLI v2 files define the training pipeline, environments and online and batch endpoints, with scripts to deploy them. A model card, a DPIA-lite, a Responsible AI assessment and a monitoring contract sit alongside the code.

architecture: A synthetic data generator feeds a training script that saves the model with its metadata and evaluation results.
FastAPI serves the model (it can also run as an Azure Functions app), and the React dashboard calls it.
Azure ML pipeline and endpoint definitions cover managed online and batch scoring, and a Power BI export produces monitoring tables.
outcome: On a held-out set of 5,000 synthetic cases the model scores 0.90 accuracy and 0.94 recall on high-priority cases (from the repo’s evaluation results).
The prediction API is live on Railway, with interactive docs at /docs.

title: Focus
summary: Local-first desktop app for planning the day, timing focused work and tracking habits, health and money, with an optional local AI helper.

brief: Focus is a desktop app that puts planning, focused work and personal tracking in one place: calendar, tasks, a focus timer, habits, health check-ins, food, money and learning. Everything is stored in a file on the computer. There’s no account to create, and sync is optional.

It started in May 2026 as a small focus-session tracker and grew over about six weeks into a full personal organiser. I built the Electron shell, the data layer, every page and an AI helper that runs on a local model by default.

built.title: Focus timer and pattern model
built.body: The timer stores start and resume times rather than counting ticks, so a running session survives the app closing. A deterministic model scores each finished session and uses the history to suggest the best hour to focus, the length of the next block and the break after it, with a plain-language reason for each suggestion.

built.title: Focus AI
built.body: A side panel turns typed requests into a plan of calendar, task, reminder and logging changes. By default it runs qwen3:4b-instruct through Ollama on the same machine; OpenAI is an opt-in alternative that also handles voice. I check every returned action against a fixed list of 18 action types and show it as a preview, and nothing is applied until it’s approved.

built.title: Personal areas and weekly review
built.body: There are pages for health check-ins, food logging with lookups against USDA FoodData Central and Open Food Facts, workouts, budgets and recurring bills, learning goals and habits. A weekly review adds these up with deterministic week-on-week totals, and the AI can write a short read-only summary on top.

built.title: Safe storage and private records
built.body: I write data to a temporary file, flush it and rename it into place, keeping the previous version as a backup that the app recovers from if the main file can’t be read. Medical records are encrypted through the operating system’s keyring with Electron’s safeStorage and are kept out of sync, exports, search and the AI.

built.title: Optional sync
built.body: Folder sync merges records by ID and last update, so two computers can share one folder without overwriting each other or a running timer. There’s also a MySQL option that stores the document per account, with passwords hashed using PBKDF2.

architecture: The Electron main process owns the data file, backups, dialogs, notifications, stored credentials, sync and every AI call. A preload script exposes a narrow window.focusDesktop API; the page runs with context isolation and no Node access.
The interface is plain ES modules with no framework: one store and reducer hold a single versioned document, and each page renders a view of it.
A schema module migrates older documents forward, including the original tracker format, every time the app loads one.
The local AI path only talks to Ollama on 127.0.0.1 and asks for JSON that matches a fixed schema. The OpenAI path uses the Responses API and stays off unless chosen.
electron-builder is configured for AppImage, Windows installer and DMG builds.

title: Phone Preview
summary: Electron developer tool that shows a mobile web app inside a realistic phone or tablet frame on the desktop, with a built-in console.

brief: A full-width browser tab doesn’t show how a mobile web app will feel on a phone. Phone Preview opens a transparent, frameless window that draws a device frame and loads the app into a screen-sized view, so it floats on the desktop like a handset.
It’s a small tool: one Electron main file and a shell launcher, released under the MIT licence.

built.title: Device presets
built.body: A dropdown holds 48 presets across iPhone, Pixel, Galaxy (including Fold and Flip screens) and iPad. Each one sets the CSS viewport, pixel ratio, corner radii and notch or Dynamic Island size, and I resize the window to fit the new frame, scaling it down if it won’t fit the screen.

built.title: Clipped app view
built.body: The app loads in an Electron webview clipped to the screen shape, so modals and fixed navigation bars stay inside the phone instead of spilling across the desktop.

built.title: Connect screen and console
built.body: A connect screen inside the phone takes any local or remote URL and has one-click buttons for common dev server ports such as Expo, Vite and Next. I forward the app’s console messages to a strip above the phone, with a panel that highlights warnings and errors.

architecture: The main process builds the shell page (frame, controls and device data) as HTML and loads it into a transparent, frameless window that can’t be resized by hand.
The app under test runs in a webview inside that page, and its console events feed the shell’s log panel.
